\section[\ar{يوم}]{\ar{يوم} (yawm) — "day," a word shared across the whole Semitic family}

\label{lesson:AR-C25-yawm}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} This word is bigger than Arabic — it's one of the oldest, most widely shared words across the entire Semitic language family.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — \ar{يوم} — "day"}
\textbf{\ar{يوم}} (\textbf{yawm}) — "\textbf{day}" — root \textbf{y-w-m}. Arabic's day-names can compound with \emph{yawm} — \textbf{\ar{يوم} \ar{الجمعة}} (\emph{yawm al-jumʿa}, "day of the gathering") is the full, formal way to say "Friday," the exact same "day-of-X" construct-state pattern as Latin's \emph{diēs Lūnae} — but colloquially, the bare day-name alone (\emph{al-jumʿa}, \emph{as-sabt}, already taught earlier) is just as common. \emph{Yawm} itself is also the ordinary, standalone word for "a day."

\begin{culture}
\textbf{Yawm} traces to \textbf{Proto-Semitic} \emph{\textbf{*yawm-}} — and this isn't just an Arabic word with foreign relatives, it's a genuinely \textbf{Common Semitic} word, found with the same shape and meaning across the whole family: Hebrew \textbf{\he{יוֹם}} (\emph{yōm} — yes, the \emph{yom} in \textbf{Yom Kippur}, "Day of Atonement"), Akkadian \textbf{ūmum}, and Aramaic \textbf{yawmā}. Four different Semitic languages, one shared ancient word for "day."
\end{culture}

\begin{culture}
Some scholars push the trail back even further, to a proposed \textbf{Proto-Afroasiatic} root, \emph{\textbf{*yam-}} ("day") — and speculatively connect it to Egyptian \textbf{ỉmy}, meaning "\textbf{sun}" (literally "the eye"). Be honest: this deeper connection is a genuinely \textbf{proposed}, citable scholarly idea within comparative Afroasiatic linguistics — but a minority one, not accepted by most Egyptologists (standard Egyptian dictionaries gloss \emph{ỉmy} as a common grammatical form, "who/which is in," not "sun," and ordinary Egyptian for "day" is an unrelated word, \emph{ḥrw}). Not settled fact the way the Semitic-family cognates are.
\end{culture}
